C0.quote: We study the parameterized complexity of counting variants of Swap- and ShiftBribery
C0.note: Counting versions of bribery problems used to assess the robustness of election winners.

C1.quote: We consider their computational complexity for parameterizations by the number
C1.note: Complexity results dominate. Experiments use synthetic (map of elections) and real cycling data.

C2.3.quote: some other voters accidently “misranked” some of the candidates
C2.3.note: The motivation refers to how voters would rank candidates apart from the votes cast. In the formal model the preference order is identified with the vote.

C2.4.note: DIST and IDU fit about equally well; DIST is listed first. The text says the cast votes may differ from what voters would rank, but the formal model uses one object (preference order = vote).

C3.1.note: Deviations from votes are random swaps or briber actions. Voters themselves are never modelled as strategic.

C3.2.note: There is only the terminological identification of preference orders with votes.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare or similar notion is used for voters.

C5.1.note: Outcomes are evaluated by robustness (winning probabilities, thresholds), not by welfare or representation.

VOT.quote_behav: Each voter vi has a preference order
VOT.note: Votes are given as exogenous input.

BRI.quote_behav: our goal is to preclude the designated candidate’s victory
BRI.quote_info: we are given an election E, a designated candidate p
BRI.note: The briber is an implicit agent performing swaps toward a goal, in the decision and minimum-cost variants. In the counting variants the swaps are counted or randomised rather than chosen.
